notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Ezekiel 20:1–24, drawing on the sources I was able to access before hitting fetch limits. Where a tradition's distinctive view appeared, I have noted it.

---

## Ezekiel 20:1–24 – Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — *"In the seventh year, on the tenth day of the fifth month, some of the elders of Israel came to inquire of the LORD, and they sat down before me."*

- **The date** is August 591/590 BC — about two years and one month after Ezekiel’s call (Ezekiel 1:2) and roughly eleven months after the visions of Ezekiel 8. The "seventh year" is reckoned from the deportation of King Jehoiachin. (EnduringWord.com; Ellicott)
- **Who came:** "Elders of Israel" — community leaders among the exiles in Babylon. They came to Ezekiel as a recognised prophet and "sat before" him, a posture of waiting for a prophetic word. Their specific question is not stated in the text, but the context suggests they were asking about their national plight and when deliverance might come. (EnduringWord.com; Pulpit Commentary)
- **Baptist note:** Garner-Howes says the elders' unspoken inquiry was probably "regarding the cause of their national calamities and how long they would continue." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-20.html)

---

### vv. 2–3 — *"Then the word of the LORD came to me… 'Have you come to inquire of Me? As surely as I live, I will not be consulted by you, declares the Lord GOD.'"*

- **God's blunt refusal:** This is similar to the earlier occasion in Ezekiel 14:3. God answers, but not with the oracle the elders wanted. Instead, He rebukes them with a solemn oath ("As I live"). (EnduringWord.com; Ellicott)
- **Why the refusal?** The elders' inquiry was hollow. As Matthew Poole (cited by EnduringWord) says: "you act a deep hypocrisy, being already resolved on your own course, and yet now pretend you would know my counsel." They wanted information, not transformation. (EnduringWord.com)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** They were "anxious for light on their fate" but "did not wish to be troubled about their sins." God had already been speaking plainly through Ezekiel, yet they had refused to listen; now they wanted fresh revelation while ignoring what had already been given. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-20.html)
- **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** The Lord's response was "irony or sarcasm" — in effect, "you really do not expect me to stoop to converse with you, do you?" They were "morally incapable of receiving knowledge," citing Psalm 66:18 and John 7:17. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-20.html)
- **St. Jerome** (cited by Ellicott): "To the holy, and to those who ask for right things, the promise is given, 'While they are yet speaking, I will say, Here I am'; but to sinners… no answer is given, but only a fierce rebuke." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/20.htm)

---

### v. 4 — *"Will you judge them, will you judge them, son of man? Confront them with the abominations of their fathers."*

- **The doubled question** is a strong imperative: "You must judge them!" Ezekiel is told to take the role of a prosecutor or judge and lay out the charges — not against the elders alone, but against the nation across its history. (EnduringWord.com; Ellicott; Pulpit Commentary)
- **"Confront them with the abominations of their fathers":** God does not allow the current generation to distance itself from the sins of previous generations. The point is that the present generation has replicated those same sins (made explicit later in the chapter). (EnduringWord.com)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The prophet is directed "to assume the office of a judge, and as such to press home upon his hearers… their own sins and those of their fathers." This is a direct historical survey rather than the figurative language of Ezekiel 16. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-20.html)

---

### v. 5 — *"On the day I chose Israel, I swore an oath to the descendants of the house of Jacob… With an uplifted hand I said to them, 'I am the LORD your God.'"*

- **"I chose Israel":** God took the initiative; Israel did not choose Him. (Garner-Howes, citing Ephesians 1:11 and John 15:16 as cross-references)
- **"Raised My hand in an oath":** The uplifted hand was the ancient gesture for swearing an oath (cf. Genesis 14:22; Deuteronomy 32:40). This refers to the covenant promises made to the patriarchs, reaffirmed in Egypt. (EnduringWord.com; Ellicott)
- **No specific Pentateuchal record** of this exact oath exists, but it summarises God's covenant commitment as expressed in passages like Exodus 6:2–8. (EnduringWord.com; Ellicott)
- **"In the land of Egypt"** — God began Israel's history, not in Canaan, but while they were still slaves. His self-revelation started there. (Ellicott)

---

### v. 6 — *"On that day I swore to bring them out… into a land that I had searched out for them, a land flowing with milk and honey, the glory of all lands."*

- **"A land that I had searched out for them":** Highly anthropomorphic language — God speaks as though He Himself scouted the land for Israel. This is a "manner of man" expression emphasising God's personal, providential care. (EnduringWord.com, citing Poole)
- **"The glory of all lands":** A phrase unique to Ezekiel (also used in v. 15; cf. Daniel 11:16). Ellicott notes that however strange this may seem today given centuries of desolation, at the time of the conquest the land fulfilled every expectation (Joshua 23:14). (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/20.htm)
- **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** Canaan was "the Land-glory center of the world" where Israel was to worship the one God alone. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-20.html)

---

### v. 7 — *"Each of you must throw away the abominations before his eyes, and you must not defile yourselves with the idols of Egypt. I am the LORD your God."*

- **A command given in Egypt:** Before the Exodus, God commanded Israel to abandon Egyptian idols. This is not explicitly narrated in Exodus, but is clearly implied. The golden calf incident (Exodus 32) and Joshua 24:14 ("Put away the gods which your fathers served… in Egypt") confirm that Israel was steeped in Egyptian idolatry. (EnduringWord.com; Ellicott; Pulpit Commentary)
- **"Abominations before his eyes":** The idols were visible, attractive objects. Israel was told to throw away what their eyes lusted after. (EnduringWord.com)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The second commandment (no graven images) directly addresses the infection of Egyptian animal-worship (Mnevis/Apis bulls) that Israel had absorbed. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-20.html)

---

### v. 8 — *"But they rebelled against Me and refused to listen. None of them cast away the abominations… So I resolved to pour out My wrath upon them… in the land of Egypt."*

- **Idolatry while still in Egypt:** Israel did not obey even this first command. EnduringWord lists evidences: the golden calf, Joshua 24:14's retrospective command, and Jeroboam's later choice of calves as worship objects — all suggesting a deep Egyptian idolatrous streak. (EnduringWord.com)
- **God's response — threatened judgment in Egypt:** God resolved (literally "said in His heart") to pour out wrath on them right there. This "half-purposing" is anthropomorphic — it describes what justice would have demanded. (EnduringWord.com; Pulpit Commentary)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** No specific narrative in the Pentateuch records this threat, but it "lies in the nature of the case." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-20.html)

---

### v. 9 — *"But I acted for the sake of My name, that it should not be profaned in the eyes of the nations…"*

- **Why God spared them:** Not because Israel deserved it, but "for My name's sake" — to protect His reputation among the nations. Had God destroyed Israel in Egypt, the Gentiles would have concluded that Yahweh was unable to deliver His people. (EnduringWord.com; Ellicott; Pulpit Commentary)
- **Feinberg** (cited by EnduringWord): "When God could find no basis in them for extending to them His mercy and grace, He did it solely for His name's sake, that is, for His own glory." (EnduringWord.com)
- **Block** (cited by EnduringWord): "The divine reputation depends on the fate and welfare of his people. All of God's dealings with Israel were public — before the eyes of the nations." (EnduringWord.com)
- **This becomes a refrain:** The phrase "for My name's sake" recurs at vv. 14, 22, forming a threefold pattern: God withheld judgment in Egypt, in the first wilderness generation, and in the second wilderness generation — each time for His reputation.
- **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** God worked "for the honor of His name (among the heathen) that the honor and integrity of His name might not be abased, defamed or brought low." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-20.html)

---

### v. 10 — *"So I brought them out of the land of Egypt and led them into the wilderness."*

- **The transition:** God did what He promised — the Exodus happened. He "made them go out" (as Clarke notes, they were not entirely willing to leave their "house of bondage"). (EnduringWord.com)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "He wrought for his Name's sake, that the deliverance of the Exodus might manifest his righteousness and might." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-20.html)
- This verse opens the second period of the historical review: the earlier wilderness period (vv. 10–17). (Ellicott)

---

### v. 11 — *"And I gave them My statutes and made known to them My ordinances — for the man who does these things will live by them."*

- **The giving of the Law at Sinai:** Ezekiel speaks of the Mosaic law with high regard, echoing Deuteronomy 30:15–20. (Ellicott; Pulpit Commentary)
- **"Will live by them":** This is a quotation from Leviticus 18:5. Ellicott explains that "what was required was not a mere outward, technical, and perfunctory keeping of certain definite precepts, but a living and loving obedience to God's will from the heart." It is not about earning eternal salvation by works but about a life of covenant faithfulness. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/20.htm)
- **EnduringWord** (citing Alexander): "It is not a reference to eternal salvation by works." The promise is of a full, blessed life under God's covenant. (EnduringWord.com)
- **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** The law did two things: (1) pointed them to acknowledge sins and trust the coming Son-Sacrifice, and (2) gave regulatory laws for civil, moral, and ethical behaviour. "Obeying His laws men should live, disobeying them they should be put to death." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-20.html)

---

### v. 12 — *"I also gave them My Sabbaths as a sign between us, so that they would know that I am the LORD who sanctifies them."*

- **The Sabbath as covenant sign:** Quoting Exodus 31:13, the Sabbath is the "central sign" or even "sacrament" of the old covenant — a mark distinguishing Israel from the nations and a means of realising the covenant relationship. (Ellicott; Pulpit Commentary)
- **"I am the LORD who sanctifies them":** The Sabbath is a sign pointing to God's work of setting His people apart. It is not merely a day of physical rest but a sign "of the covenant, and a means of realising it in the study of God's word, and the communion of the soul with Him." (Ellicott)
- **Feinberg** (cited by EnduringWord): "The Sabbath was the central sign of the old covenant. Repeatedly it is shown that the law of the Sabbath was not legislation by which they could gain life but rather the sign of the covenant between God and Israel." (EnduringWord.com)
- **Ellicott adds:** The Sabbath, like circumcision, was older than Moses (cf. John 7:22), but was "now commanded anew, and made the especial pledge of the covenant." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/20.htm)

---

### v. 13 — *"Yet the house of Israel rebelled against Me in the wilderness. They did not follow My statutes and they rejected My ordinances… and they utterly profaned My Sabbaths…"*

- **Rebellion in the wilderness:** Multiple instances are in view — the golden calf (Exodus 32), the refusal to enter Canaan (Numbers 14), and Baal-Peor (Numbers 25). (Ellicott; EnduringWord)
- **Sabbath profanation:** Only two explicit Sabbath violations are recorded in the Torah (Exodus 16:27; Numbers 15:32), but the prophets looked beneath the surface: a merely formal observance that did not truly sanctify the day was itself a pollution. (Ellicott; Pulpit Commentary)
- **Barnes:** The pollution was "not by actual non-observance of the sabbatical rest in the wilderness, but in failing to make the day holy in deed as well as in name by earnest worship and true heart service." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/ezekiel-20.html)
- **The refrain:** "though the man who does these things will live by them" — repeated at vv. 13, 21, underscoring the tragedy: life was held out to them, but they chose death. (EnduringWord.com)

---

### v. 14 — *"But I acted for the sake of My name, so that it would not be profaned in the eyes of the nations in whose sight I had brought them out."*

- **Second occurrence of the refrain:** Just as in Egypt (v. 9), God restrained His wrath in the wilderness for the sake of His reputation. Ellicott notes this echoes Moses' own intercessory plea (Exodus 32:12; Numbers 14:13–16; Deuteronomy 9:28). (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/20.htm)

---

### vv. 15–16 — *"Moreover, with an uplifted hand I swore to them in the wilderness that I would not bring them into the land… because they kept rejecting My ordinances… for their hearts continually went after their idols."*

- **The oath of exclusion:** This refers to Numbers 14:28–29, where God swore that the generation that came out of Egypt (aged twenty and above) would die in the wilderness and not enter Canaan. (Ellicott; EnduringWord)
- **The reason — idolatrous hearts:** Though outward idolatry may have been suppressed at times, "their heart went after their idols." Trapp (cited by EnduringWord) calls them "dungy deities" — a reference to the Hebrew term for idols as something detestable. (EnduringWord.com)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The Baal-Peor incident (Numbers 25:3–9) showed how readily idolatrous tendencies erupted into act. Amos 5:25–26 implies a tradition of similar acts throughout the wilderness period. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-20.html)

---

### v. 17 — *"Yet I looked on them with pity and did not destroy them or bring them to an end in the wilderness."*

- **"My eye spared them":** Even when the adults were barred from Canaan, God did not annihilate the nation. The next generation was preserved. (EnduringWord.com)
- **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** God spared them "because of His everlasting covenant with Abraham. His fidelity to His covenant stands in stark contrast with their murmuring, whining, and rebellion." He also notes the intercession of Moses who "stood in the gap" (Psalm 106:23–24; Exodus 32:30–35). (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-20.html)

---

### vv. 18–20 — *"In the wilderness I said to their children: 'Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers or keep their ordinances… I am the LORD your God; walk in My statutes… Keep My Sabbaths holy, that they may be a sign between us…'"*

- **The appeal to the second generation:** The Book of Deuteronomy is essentially the commentary on these verses — Moses' exhortation to the children of the rebels to obey where their fathers failed. (Ellicott; Pulpit Commentary)
- **"Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers":** This is striking — the "statutes" of the fathers here are not God's law but the fathers' own idolatrous patterns. The children are told to reject the family tradition of rebellion. (EnduringWord.com)
- **The positive command (vv. 19–20):** The threefold call — walk in My statutes, keep My ordinances, hallow My Sabbaths — mirrors the threefold sin of the fathers (v. 13, 16). The Sabbath remains the central covenant sign. (Ellicott; EnduringWord)
- **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** The Sabbath was to be held sacred "that they might exist as a sign between Him and them, that they be preserved from destruction and prospered in spiritual ways." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-20.html)

---

### vv. 21–22 — *"But the children rebelled against Me. They did not walk in My statutes… So I resolved to pour out My wrath upon them… But I withheld My hand and acted for the sake of My name…"*

- **The second generation also rebelled:** The children raised in the wilderness proved no better than their fathers. The history of the later wilderness period and even the conquest and judges periods bears this out. (EnduringWord.com; Ellicott)
- **Third occurrence of the "for My name's sake" refrain (v. 22):** God withholds His hand yet again. The pattern is relentless: rebellion → threatened judgment → mercy for His name's sake → rebellion. This triple refrain (vv. 9, 14, 22) structures the entire historical review. (EnduringWord.com)
- **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** The children's rebellion included Sabbath-breaking (Numbers 15:32), Korah's rebellion (Numbers 16–17), and other acts. God chastened them severely. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-20.html)

---

### v. 23 — *"However, with an uplifted hand I swore to them in the wilderness that I would scatter them among the nations and disperse them throughout the lands."*

- **The scattering oath:** This is the commuted sentence — instead of immediate destruction, dispersion. The oath is rooted in Leviticus 26:33 and Deuteronomy 4:27; 28:64. (Ellicott; EnduringWord)
- **Ellicott:** This threat was "not designed to be fulfilled in that immediate generation" but was given to that generation as representing the nation. It was a long-range warning, now being fulfilled in Ezekiel's day through the Babylonian exile. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/20.htm)
- **Feinberg** (cited by EnduringWord): "But even as early as the wilderness era God had predicted Israel's worldwide scattering among the nations (Deuteronomy 28:64–68). The Babylonian captivity was only a partial realization of this prophecy by Moses." This points toward a still-future, fuller scattering. (EnduringWord.com)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Ezekiel saw this oath as the "commutation of the sentence of destruction for that of the dispersion," leaving the time and manner to God's will. Partial dispersions had occurred throughout the period of the judges and monarchy; the exile was the culmination. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-20.html)

---

### v. 24 — *"For they did not practice My ordinances, but they rejected My statutes and profaned My Sabbaths, fixing their eyes on the idols of their fathers."*

- **The threefold indictment:** (1) rejected God's statutes, (2) profaned His Sabbaths, (3) lusted after idols ("fixing their eyes" — literally, their eyes were after their fathers' idols). This matches the threefold sin-pattern throughout the chapter. (EnduringWord.com; Ellicott)
- **"The idols of their fathers":** The tragedy is that each generation adopted the sins of the previous one, despite God's repeated warnings and fresh starts. The "eyes" fixed on idols contrasts with eyes that should have been fixed on God and His Sabbaths. (EnduringWord.com)
- **Ellicott** (on the broader passage): The elders who came to Ezekiel in v. 1 were now being told that the scattering they were experiencing was not a surprise or an accident — it was the fulfilment of an oath sworn long ago, the just penalty for sins that spanned their entire national history. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/20.htm)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

The major theological distinctives on this passage cluster around a few key themes:

### 1. "The man who does these things will live by them" (vv. 11, 13, 21)

- **Reformed / Lutheran:** Typically see this as expressing the law's genuine (if hypothetical) promise — life through perfect obedience — which simultaneously exposes human inability and drives us to Christ. The law is "holy, just, and good" (Romans 7:12) and the fault lies not in the law but in sinful humanity.
- **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** Emphasises that the law pointed Israel to "trust His coming Son-Sacrifice to save them" — a Christocentric reading from the start. The law also provided regulatory civil and moral guidance for the nation. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-20.html)
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (EnduringWord):** Explicitly states this is "not a reference to eternal salvation by works" but to temporal covenant blessing and fullness of life. (EnduringWord.com)

### 2. The Sabbath as "a sign" (vv. 12, 20)

- **Reformed (covenant theology):** Often sees the Sabbath as a creation ordinance (Genesis 2:2–3) that predates Moses, now functioning as a covenant sign for Israel. Its abiding moral substance transfers to the Lord's Day in the new covenant.
- **Lutheran:** Typically sees the Sabbath as a ceremonial law given specifically to Israel, not binding on Gentile Christians in its Old Testament form, though the principle of rest and worship remains valuable.
- **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** States broadly that "the people or land that disregards this principle of sabbath rest and worship will surely come to decay" — treating the Sabbath principle as universally applicable. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-20.html)
- **Seventh-day Adventist** (not in retrieved sources but well-known): Would emphasise that the Sabbath remains the unchanged sign between God and His people, pointing to a literal seventh-day observance.

### 3. "For My name's sake" (vv. 9, 14, 22)

- **Reformed:** Heavily emphasises this as central to the doctrine of God's sovereignty and self-glorification. God's ultimate motivation in withholding judgment is His own glory and reputation — a theme dear to Reformed theology.
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (EnduringWord):** Stresses the same point through Feinberg and Block: God's reputation among the nations is at stake. (EnduringWord.com)

### 4. The "scattering" oath (v. 23)

- **Dispensational (traditional):** Sees this as a prophecy with multiple fulfilments — the Babylonian exile was a partial fulfilment, but a worldwide scattering and regathering still awaits ethnic Israel. EnduringWord (Pentecostal/Charismatic, with dispensational leanings) cites Feinberg that "the Babylonian captivity was only a partial realization." (EnduringWord.com)
- **Covenant/Reformed:** Typically sees the scattering as fulfilled in the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles, with the "regathering" fulfilled spiritually in Christ and the church as the true Israel, though some Reformed (postmillennial or historic premillennial) allow for a future national restoration.
